title: Care for creation
hook: a saint sings to Brother Sun and Sister Water, and a pope borrows his first words

segments.voice: Yesterday, solidarity: one body, made of one. Your line was one family. Did someone far away become, for a moment, a cousin you haven't met? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon. Brother Wind. Sister Water. In his Canticle of the Creatures, Francis of Assisi praises God for each of them by name, as if he were introducing his relatives. Then he calls the earth itself our sister and mother, who feeds us. Stanza after stanza, the canticle repeats the same words in the old Italian of his day: laudato si', praise be to you. When Pope Francis wrote a letter about the environment, he took its name from that refrain, and its subtitle reads: on care for our common home. Today, care for creation.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER WATER.` → `THE EARTH: SISTER AND MOTHER.` → `LAUDATO SI'.`

segments.voice: First, the goodness. Genesis looks back over everything made, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." Very good, and the verse gives no reason but that God made them. In Catholic teaching, creation has worth because God made it, not only because people need it. Second, who owns it. A psalm says, in the Douay-Rheims: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof." People are tenants, not landlords. The Catechism says the dominion Genesis gives humanity isn't absolute. It's a trust, and it has to respect the integrity of creation. Third, the earth and the poor together. Pope Francis wrote that damage to the environment falls hardest on the most vulnerable, and he asked his readers to hear both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor. A poisoned river is an injustice to whoever lives downstream. So care for creation isn't a separate cause sitting beside the rest of this block; it's dignity, the poor and solidarity, all at once, with soil and water in the picture. Fourth, time. Our common home is shared not only across the globe but across the years. The Catechism names the generations to come, and Pope Francis wrote that the world we've received belongs also to those who will follow us. Somebody not yet born will drink from the same river. That's who the carry has in mind.
screen: `VERY GOOD, BECAUSE GOD MADE IT.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `THE CRY OF THE EARTH AND THE POOR.` · then: `A HOME FOR THOSE NOT YET BORN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: save water today. Settle, and breathe. Sister Water, Francis called it. Let the water you'll use today come to mind: the shower, the sink, the kettle, the dishes, the glass by your bed. Pick one place to use less, and decide exactly how. A shorter shower. The tap off while you brush. A full load instead of half. Then let your mind follow that water downstream, to the people and the creatures who share it, now and later. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Care for creation. In Catholic teaching, the earth is the Lord's, very good in itself, and held in trust for the poor and for generations to come. Today's word.
Your line: our common home. Today, each time you turn on a tap, remember who's downstream, and save a little. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics read Pope Francis's Laudato Si' in parishes and schools, some keep a Season of Creation in the fall, and Francis of Assisi's canticle is prayed and sung around his feast day.
